text: So our annual report 2020, I hope you've all got a chance to see it. We've sent it there. We've of course been adapting to the pandemic. It's a tough year for everyone, certainly a difficult year to provide municipal services, including library services. Throughout this, the library has felt the sort of tension between, on the one hand, libraries have really great free resources and collections and services that have a lot of value during the pandemic when people are staying home and they're socially isolated. But on the other hand, we're a public space where our community members access it directly. So there are safety considerations. Libraries have had to limit access to our resources. Buildings were shut down in the spring and again recently. And libraries continue to limit programs and gatherings and numbers in the building. And also there are certain members of community who are not yet comfortable returning to the library even when we are open. So to balance these considerations and meet the community's needs, the library's been very active in adapting and finding new ways to provide our services in spite of these difficulties. The bad news, of course, is that because of the shutdown, because of everything, our use statistics for 2020 are way down. Visits, internet use in the library, program participation all down around half. Circulation is down, although not quite as much. It's more like 20, 25%. And so it's worth noting that that's not quite as far down. And we'll talk about that in a second. When we adapted, our service adaptations have included curbside pickup, which it was a new thing. All the libraries are doing that now. We're able to do that. And our photos, the first day that we started back in May, I had a list of people who said, call me as soon as you can do this. And I had all these packs waiting for people when we opened. And there were a couple of kids who were so excited to get, their mom sent us a picture because they were so excited to get the library books. They just kind of got in the door, wouldn't even take off their coat before they got at them. So that was nice to see. We've had to reorganize our space to support distancing. We're quarantining returned books. Kind of a barrier at the front desk. And we've had enhanced cleaning for computers and for the whole building. And we've had our sort of different services. Jigsaw puzzles are much more popular now. We've had contactless browsing, Windows displays. We've been waiving overdue fines because of the difficulty people bring back and all that sort of thing. One of the things, reasons our circulation's not down quite as much is because of our online services, which saw big increases during the pandemic, really brought them to people's attentions. Use in our e-books and e-audiobooks jumped 35%, started in the spring. And also our Canopy film streaming service, that went up by quite a lot as well. And there were other e-resources. Some vendors during spring provided free access through libraries, which was very nice. We also were still able to be in the building because it was just sort of one of us at a time to provide support by email or phone to help people with these services. And they've continued to be popular even throughout this all and still. And speaking of going online, some of our programs went online. Since we can't do in-person programming in meetings, it's pretty much off the table. We got a Zoom subscription originally to let our board continue to meet, but we've also been providing a virtual meeting space for the public. It's been successful for our adult programs, such as Off the Shelf and our Sketchy art group, but also for book clubs have been meeting that way and some community groups. And this wasn't involved Zoom, but it was an online thing. Diana Beresford Kroger, who is actually a world famous scientist who lives in Wolford area. She would usually be traveling to a lot of conferences and things. And of course she wasn't able to do that. So she was able to attend virtually and do her talks from the library, which was kind of exciting for us. And so that's been very successful this year. With our children's program, with the kids programs that we did do online stories, all started in April and we're still doing them. Every week I post a story. My cat has helped me with a few of them, as you can see in the picture. And with that, there's been a real interest in having something a little bit more in-person. So in the summer we did outdoor story time. So we could sort of spread out. We've had some like low numbers for story time in the library over the winter. And we have a lot of distancing and things like that. That's been popular. Our summer reading club, we continue to do the prize draw, which is extremely popular, but we shifted to more online content and take-home crafts rather than our regular programs. At Christmas and Halloween, we started using our green screen to do some pictures, even though people couldn't go anywhere, couldn't go see Santa, we could make it look like they did. And we had some little activity craft stations and stories through the library. And so our building is fairly large, so we could spread them out in different places and give the kids a little map and then go from station to station. And that's been popular. And a lot of parents really liked that there's like a little something for the kids to do, because especially for little kids, it's been so shut down for them for the past year. And that's really a long time when you're two or three years old. We've also... Every store we work together with our guests. And some of them have been on the back burner for the past year, visits and loans to the school and the daycare and play group, of course, and loans to senior homes, passes to the museums. Like in February of last year, they did a Village Chef Dinner, which was very successful, which was lucky because pretty much all their other fundraisers had to be canceled, but they had enough money to support the programs and activities and services that they usually do.
